GraceChangeDesignContext.Rationale:
Worldline's capability model separates contract definition, provider publication, capability discovery, authorization, and invocation. Multiple installations of a single PluginDefinition can exist with separate installation-owned configuration.
During the early feasibility gate (Task T-001) of C-BROWSER-SEARCH-PROVIDERS-20260904, an architectural gap in `worldline-kernel` was verified: while `discover_capabilities_for` enumerates all active installations, `CapabilityRegistry::resolve` and `InvocationBroker::invoke` unconditionally execute default deterministic resolution ("highest-compatible-minor; installation-id; runtime-id"). As a result, when two installations of the same capability are simultaneously active, the candidate with the higher InstallationId is shadowed and cannot be invoked.
Rather than adding search-specific or browser-specific router workarounds, the project exercises the early feasibility STOP/REPLAN gate to enhance the generic platform primitive in `worldline-kernel`.
GraceChangeDesignContext.ArchitectureSketch: Caller | +---> capability_for(caller, cap) | | | v | CapabilityTarget::AnyCompatible | | | v | Deterministic default resolution (minor -> installation_id -> runtime_id) | +---> capability_for_installation(caller, cap, target_installation) | v CapabilityTarget::Installation(target_installation) | v Exact matching active provider for target_installation | +---> if active & compatible: invoke current live RuntimeId +---> if missing / stopped / incompatible / quarantined: fail closed (TargetUnavailable)

KeyDesignDecisions.Decision: Target durable InstallationId, not ephemeral RuntimeId. RuntimeId changes upon restart, crash, or reload. The broker must resolve the live RuntimeId at invocation admission time.

No preferred-provider table or selection persistence in the microkernel. The kernel provides the generic mechanism ("invoke capability X on installation Y"); policy and preference persistence belong to caller/shell/profile layers.

Strict failure semantics with zero silent fallback. If a targeted installation is absent, stopped, quarantined, or incompatible, the invocation must fail explicitly. A silent fallback to the default provider would break caller assumptions and security boundaries.
Targeting conveys zero authority. The caller must possess standard capability authorization for the capability contract and operation.
Clean backward compatibility: the existing `capability_for(caller, capability)` maps to `CapabilityTarget::AnyCompatible` and preserves unchanged deterministic resolution.

Alternatives.Alternative: Add a preferred-provider table / set_preferred_provider API in the kernel. Rejected because default provider selection is user/profile/shell policy. The microkernel must remain policy-free and generic.
Target ephemeral RuntimeId directly. Rejected because RuntimeId is transient and does not survive restart or crash recovery. Durable targeting must use InstallationId.

Silent fallback to default provider on target failure. Rejected because explicit targeting must be deterministic and failure-transparent. Silent fallback could lead to unexpected behavior and confused-deputy issues.

Intermediary router/proxy plugin in userland. Rejected because multi-install invocation is a fundamental platform primitive. Hiding it behind an ad-hoc router would create architectural debt and obscure the contract.

SecurityAndPrivacy.Point: Targeting does not grant privilege. Invocations targeted to a specific installation still require ordinary capability authorization grants.
Restart or replacement of a target installation produces a fresh RuntimeId. Ephemeral security tokens and live authorities are never inherited from the old runtime.
Trajectory audit logs record capability ID, requested target InstallationId, resolved RuntimeId, and outcome code, without logging request/response payloads.

DeferredDecisions.Decision: Persistent preference storage and user default selection mechanisms are deferred to shell and workspace service layers.

Scenarios.Scenario: Two installations of `worldline-browser-search` (A and B) are active. A caller invoking with CapabilityTarget::Installation(B) successfully executes on installation B, even if A has a lower InstallationId.
Targeted installation B crashes and is restarted by the runtime supervisor. A subsequent invocation targeted to B resolves to B's new RuntimeId and succeeds without stale authority inheritance.
Targeted installation B is quarantined. An invocation targeted to B fails immediately with `TargetUnavailable` and does NOT fallback to installation A.
